learn.hook: Over the bridge, through the tunnel, along the river — tiny words guide every journey!
points: A preposition shows how a noun or pronoun is related to another word, often by place, direction or time.
Place: in, on, under, between, beside, near, behind, at.
Direction or movement: to, towards, into, across, along, through, up, down.
'In' shows position inside; 'into' shows movement from outside to inside.
'Between' is used for two people or things; 'among' for more than two.

example.q: Fill the blanks: 'The ferry went ___ the river, and we walked ___ the bank to the temple.'
steps: Going from one side to the other side → across
Moving beside the length of the bank → along
example.answer: across, along

learn.reallife: Maps, signboards and GPS directions use prepositions: 'Turn left at the signal, go across the bridge.'

items.text: The cat is hiding ___ the bed.
Meena sat ___ her two friends.
The children ran ___ the park towards the gate.
Hang the calendar ___ the wall.

games.title: Preposition rules
items: 'Between' is used for two people or things.
'Into' shows movement from outside to inside.
'Among' is used for exactly two things.
'Among' is for more than two; 'between' is for two.
In 'The cat is under the bed', 'under' is a preposition.
It shows where the cat is.
'Quickly' is an adverb; it tells how something is done.

quiz.q: 'The boat sailed ___ the river to the other bank.'
quiz.explain: Across means from one side to the other.
steps: The boat goes from one bank to the other.
'Across' means from one side to the other.
So the answer is 'across'.
Answer: across
quiz.mistake: Picks a place word instead of a direction word

quiz.q: 'The cat ran ___ the house when it started raining.'
quiz.explain: 'Into' shows movement from outside to inside.
steps: The cat moves from outside to inside the house.
'Into' shows movement from outside to inside ('in' shows only position).
So the answer is 'into'.
Answer: into
quiz.mistake: Does not use the movement preposition

quiz.q: 'The ball is ___ the table and the chair.'
quiz.explain: Two things are named, so we use 'between'.
steps: Two things are named: the table and the chair.
'Between' is used for two; 'among' for more than two.
So the answer is 'between'.
Answer: between
quiz.mistake: Uses 'among' for two things

quiz.q: 'Share the sweets ___ all your classmates.'
quiz.explain: There are many classmates (more than two), so 'among' is correct.
steps: 'All your classmates' means more than two people.
'Among' is used for more than two.
So the answer is 'among'.
Answer: among
quiz.mistake: Uses 'between' for a big group

quiz.q: 'We waited ___ the bus stop for half an hour.'
quiz.explain: 'At' is used for a particular point or place like a bus stop.
steps: A bus stop is a particular point or place.
We use 'at' for such points.
So the answer is 'at'.
Answer: at
quiz.mistake: Uses a movement preposition for a fixed point

quiz.q: 'My cousin lives ___ Kolkata.'
quiz.explain: We use 'in' for cities and countries.
steps: Kolkata is a city.
We use 'in' for cities and countries.
So the answer is 'in'.
Answer: in
quiz.mistake: Uses a preposition that shows movement or surface

quiz.q: 'The train went ___ a long tunnel.'
quiz.explain: 'Through' means in at one end and out at the other.
steps: A train enters a tunnel at one end and comes out at the other.
'Through' means in at one end and out at the other.
So the answer is 'through'.
Answer: through
quiz.mistake: Does not picture the movement

quiz.q: 'Walk ___ the river bank to reach the temple.'
quiz.explain: 'Along' means moving beside the length of something.
steps: We walk beside the length of the river bank.
'Along' means moving beside the length of something.
So the answer is 'along'.
Answer: along
quiz.mistake: Mixes up along and among

teach.ask: Gappu is lost! Explain prepositions so he can follow directions like 'across the bridge' and 'along the road'.
teach.praise: Across the bridge, along the road, into my nest — home at last!
teach.nudge: What do prepositions tell us — about place or direction?

At a point (at the bus stop); in a city (in Kolkata); through a tunnel

Don't use 'in' for movement into a place; use 'into'

learn.hook: What's waiting at the other end of a dark tunnel? Adventure stories keep you guessing!
points: 'The Tunnel' is an adventure story set around a railway tunnel in a forest. Here is our own short adventure.
An adventure story has excitement, a challenge or danger, and a character who shows courage.
Story elements: setting, characters, problem (conflict), climax (most exciting point) and resolution (how it ends).
Writers build suspense with short sentences, sound words and unanswered questions.
Courage does not mean feeling no fear — it means facing your fear.

example.q: Read: The moment the train entered the tunnel, the whole compartment went black. Ishaan gripped the window bar. The wheels roared, and his heart drummed fast. He counted slowly — one, two, three… At twenty, a burst of green and gold light flooded in: paddy fields and a sparkling river. "That wasn't scary at all," he grinned. What is the problem, the climax and the resolution?
steps: Problem: the dark tunnel makes Ishaan scared.
Climax: the roaring darkness while he counts.
Resolution: light floods in and he smiles — his fear is gone.
example.answer: Problem — fear of the dark tunnel; climax — the roaring dark while he counts; resolution — the bright fields appear and he grins.

learn.reallife: Train journeys through the Western Ghats pass through many tunnels — a real-life mini adventure!

games.title: Ishaan's journey
items: The train enters the tunnel and it goes dark.
He counts slowly to calm himself.
Green and gold light floods in.
He grins: it wasn't scary at all.

games.title: Story elements
items: The climax is the most exciting point of a story.
It is the high point of tension.
The resolution comes at the very beginning of a story.
The resolution comes at the end, when the problem is solved.
Short sentences can help build suspense.
They make the reader read faster and feel tense.
The setting tells us where and when a story takes place.
Here the setting is a train in a tunnel.
A brave person never feels any fear.
Brave people may feel afraid but still face the challenge.

quiz.q: 'The moment the train entered the tunnel, the whole compartment went black.' What is the setting?
options: A train passing through a tunnel
quiz.explain: The story takes place inside a train compartment in a tunnel.
steps: The setting is where and when a story happens.
The line says the train entered the tunnel and the compartment went black.
So the setting is a train passing through a tunnel.
Answer: A train passing through a tunnel
quiz.mistake: Does not use the place words in the text

quiz.q: 'Ishaan gripped the window bar.' This shows that he felt:
quiz.explain: Gripping something tightly is a sign of nervousness.
steps: Gripping something tightly is a sign of fear or worry.
The compartment had just gone dark.
So Ishaan felt nervous.
Answer: nervous
quiz.mistake: Does not infer a feeling from an action

quiz.q: 'The wheels roared, and his heart drummed fast.' What does 'his heart drummed fast' mean?
quiz.explain: Like fast drumbeats, his heart was beating quickly with fear and excitement.
steps: Drums beat fast and loud.
'His heart drummed fast' means his heart was beating like quick drumbeats, from fear and excitement.
So it means his heart was beating quickly.
Answer: His heart was beating quickly
quiz.mistake: Takes the description literally

quiz.q: 'He counted slowly — one, two, three…' Why did Ishaan count?
options: To calm himself in the dark
quiz.explain: Counting slowly helps you stay calm when you are afraid.
steps: Ishaan was afraid in the dark tunnel.
Counting slowly helps a person stay calm when afraid.
So he counted to calm himself in the dark.
Answer: To calm himself in the dark
quiz.mistake: Misses the purpose of the action

quiz.q: 'A burst of green and gold light flooded in: paddy fields and a sparkling river.' What did Ishaan see?

learn.hook: 'I was waiting when the train came.' — two past tenses in one sentence, working as a team!
points: Simple past tells about a finished action: The train arrived at six.
Past continuous (was/were + verb-ing) tells about an action in progress in the past: I was waiting.
Together: 'While we were waiting, the train arrived.' The longer action is past continuous; the short one that interrupts is simple past.
Use 'was' with I, he, she, it and singular nouns; 'were' with you, we, they and plural nouns.

topics.title: A poem of longing to travel

learn.hook: Have you ever heard a train at night and wondered where it was going?
points: 'Travel' is a poem in which the speaker hears trains and longs to go on a journey. Here is our own poem on that feeling.
Longing means a strong wish for something you do not have.
The speaker is the voice in the poem (the 'I'); it may or may not be the poet.
Mood is the feeling a poem creates — here it is dreamy and restless.
Poets use personification ('a whistle calls my name') and similes ('like flame') to show feelings.

example.q: Read: Each night a far-off whistle calls my name, / The lights of passing trains go by like flame. / My books stay open, but my thoughts have flown / To mountain roads and towns I've never known. How does the speaker feel, and which words show it?
steps: 'calls my name' — the speaker feels the journey is calling.
'my thoughts have flown' — the mind is already far away.
'towns I've never known' — a wish to see new places.
example.answer: The speaker feels a restless longing to travel; 'calls my name', 'thoughts have flown' and 'towns I've never known' show it.

learn.reallife: Looking at a map, a travel show or an aeroplane in the sky and wishing you were going somewhere — that's longing!

learn.hook: Close your eyes: 'hot, crispy pakoras on a rainy evening'. Can you smell them? That's imagery!
points: Imagery is language that helps us see, hear, smell, taste or feel something in our minds.

Smell imagery: 'the scent of wet earth'. Taste: 'tangy chaat'. Touch: 'the cold window glass'.
Strong imagery uses exact nouns, vivid adjectives and strong verbs.
Compare: 'The train went.' with 'The train thundered over the iron bridge.'

learn.hook: Add '-ation' to 'determine' and you get the one word every mountaineer needs: determination!
points: Determination is a strong will to reach your goal, even when it is hard.
Suffixes are added at the end of a word and can change its class: determine → determination, achieve → achievement.
-ous, -ful and -less make adjectives: courage → courageous, hope → hopeful, fear → fearless. (-ful = full of; -less = without)
-ly makes many adverbs: brave → bravely, tireless → tirelessly.
A character's actions show their qualities: trying again every day shows determination.

example.q: Read: When Pema first tried to climb the hill behind her school in Sikkim, she stopped halfway, out of breath. The next morning, she tried again. Every day she climbed a little higher, carrying her water bottle and a smile. By winter, she reached the top without stopping and saw the snowy peaks glowing in the sun. Which quality does Pema show, and which words prove it?

'The next morning, she tried again.' and 'Every day she climbed a little higher.'
She did not give up until she reached the top.

learn.hook: 'She has climbed Everest!' — the present perfect connects a past action to right now.
points: Present perfect = has/have + past participle: She has climbed. They have reached.
Use 'has' with he, she, it and singular nouns; 'have' with I, you, we, they and plural nouns.
It is used for actions finished at an unstated time or with a result now; words like just, already, yet, ever, never go with it.
Do not use it with a definite past time (yesterday, in 1953) — use simple past: 'Tenzing and Hillary reached the summit in 1953.'
'Since' + a point of time (since 2019); 'for' + a length of time (for six months).

example.q: Choose correctly: 'Riya (has reached / reached) base camp yesterday.'

The present perfect is not used with a definite past time.

games.title: Present perfect rules
items: 'Has' is used with he, she and it.
He has climbed; she has climbed.
The present perfect uses has/have + past participle.
For example: have seen, has gone.
'I have climbed the hill yesterday' is correct.
With 'yesterday' we use simple past: 'I climbed the hill yesterday.'
'Since' is used with a point of time, like 'since Monday'.
'For' is used with a length of time.
'Went' is the simple past; the past participle is 'gone'.

quiz.q: 'Riya ___ just reached base camp.'
quiz.explain: Riya is singular, so we use 'has' + reached.
steps: Present perfect = has/have + past participle.
'Riya' is singular, so use 'has': has just reached.
So the answer is 'has'.
Answer: has
quiz.mistake: Uses 'have' with a singular subject

quiz.q: 'We ___ climbed this hill many times.'
quiz.explain: 'We' takes 'have' in the present perfect.
steps: Present perfect = has/have + past participle.
'We' takes 'have': we have climbed.
So the answer is 'have'.
Answer: have
quiz.mistake: Uses 'has' with a plural subject

quiz.q: Which sentence about the 1953 climb is correct?

Tenzing and Hillary reaching the summit in 1953.
Tenzing and Hillary reached the summit in 1953.
quiz.explain: 'In 1953' is a definite past time, so simple past is used.
steps: 'In 1953' is a definite past time.
With a definite past time, use the simple past, not the present perfect.

Answer: Tenzing and Hillary reached the summit in 1953.
quiz.mistake: Uses present perfect with a definite past time

quiz.q: 'I have lived in Shimla ___ 2020.'

'Since' goes with a point of time; 'for' with a length of time.
So the answer is 'since'.
Answer: since
quiz.mistake: Mixes up since and for

quiz.q: 'The team has trained ___ three months.'

'For' goes with a length of time; 'since' with a point of time.
So the answer is 'for'.
Answer: for
quiz.mistake: Uses 'since' with a length of time

quiz.q: What is the past participle of 'go'?
quiz.explain: go – went – gone. 'Gone' goes with has/have.
steps: The forms of 'go' are go – went – gone.

quiz.q: Which sentence is in the present perfect tense?

quiz.mistake: Confuses present perfect with simple past

quiz.q: 'Have you ever ___ snow?'
quiz.explain: After 'have', we need the past participle: see – saw – seen.

see – saw – seen, so the past participle is 'seen'.

Answer: seen

chapters.title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers

learn.hook: Whether it is snowy mountains, deep seas or the open sky, someone is keeping watch over India every minute.
points: 'A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers' honours the men and women who protect our country. Homage means deep respect shown to honour someone.
India's armed forces are the Army (land), the Navy (sea) and the Air Force (air).
The President of India is the Supreme Commander of the armed forces.
Army Day is on 15 January, Air Force Day on 8 October and Navy Day on 4 December.
Soldiers also help people during floods, earthquakes and other disasters with rescue and relief.

example.q: A flood hits a village. Which forces might help, and how?
steps: The Army can rescue people and set up relief camps.
The Navy can send boats and divers.
The Air Force can fly helicopters to drop food and lift people to safety.
example.answer: All three can help: the Army on land, the Navy with boats and divers, and the Air Force with helicopters.

learn.hook: 'Param Vir' means 'the bravest of the brave' — the name of India's highest wartime gallantry award.
points: Patriotism means love for one's country; a patriot is a person who loves and serves the country.
Sacrifice means giving up something precious for the sake of others.
Gallantry and valour both mean great bravery. Valiant means very brave; its opposite is cowardly.
The Param Vir Chakra is India's highest wartime gallantry award; the Ashoka Chakra is the highest peacetime gallantry award.
The National War Memorial in New Delhi honours soldiers who gave their lives for the nation.

learn.hook: 'The soldier saved the child' or 'The child was saved by the soldier' — same event, different focus!
points: In the active voice, the subject does the action: The soldiers built the bridge.
In the passive voice, the subject receives the action: The bridge was built by the soldiers.
Passive = a form of 'be' + past participle (+ by the doer).
Simple present passive: is/are + past participle. Simple past passive: was/were + past participle.
We use the passive when the doer is unknown or less important: The fort was built long ago.

example.q: Change to passive: 'The Navy rescued the fishermen.'
steps: Object 'the fishermen' becomes the subject.

options: The soldiers were built by the bridge.

The bridge is building by the soldiers.

steps: Active: The soldiers (doer) built the bridge (object).
Passive: the object becomes the subject; past tense → was + built; add 'by the soldiers'.

Answer: The bridge was built by the soldiers.

quiz.q: Change to passive: 'The army helps the villagers.'
options: The villagers is helped by the army.
The army is helped by the villagers.
The villagers are helped by the army.
The villagers were helped by the army.
quiz.explain: Simple present with a plural subject → are + helped.
steps: The new subject 'the villagers' is plural.
Simple present passive = are + past participle: are helped.
So the passive is 'The villagers are helped by the army.'
Answer: The villagers are helped by the army.

topics.title: The queen who fought the Portuguese

learn.hook: Over 450 years ago, a queen of a small coastal kingdom in Karnataka refused to bow to a powerful European navy!
points: Rani Abbakka Chowta ruled Ullal, a port town near Mangaluru on the coast of present-day Karnataka, in the 16th century.
The Portuguese came to India by sea; Vasco da Gama reached Kozhikode (Calicut) in 1498, and the Portuguese captured Goa in 1510.
The Portuguese wanted to control the ports and the spice trade and demanded tribute (payment) from local rulers.
Rani Abbakka refused to pay and fought them for many years. She is remembered as 'Abhaya Rani' — the fearless queen.
She is honoured as one of the earliest Indian rulers to resist European powers.

example.q: Why did the Portuguese want Ullal, and how did Rani Abbakka respond?

learn.hook: A true leader is not the loudest person in the room — it's the one people trust to find a way.
points: A leader guides a group, makes decisions and takes responsibility.
Good leaders show courage, honesty, fairness, calmness and teamwork, and they listen to others.
Courage can be quiet too — like standing up for what is right.
A character's actions reveal their qualities: we don't need to be told someone is a leader if we see them lead.

example.q: Read: When the school fair got rained out, class monitor Leela did not panic. learn.hook: 'And', 'but', 'so', 'because' — joining words are the glue of good sentences!
points: Conjunctions are joining words that join words, phrases or sentences.
'And' adds; 'but' shows contrast; 'or' gives a choice; 'so' shows a result; 'because' gives a reason.
'Although' (or 'though') shows contrast inside one sentence: Although the enemy was strong, the queen did not give up.

'Until' means up to the time when: Wait here until I come back.
